Below and behind, the owner doubles over laughing and the dachshund barks. The shot ends mid-stride, the cat still racing toward the lens.

PERFORMANCE

The cat is fully expressive in a natural feline way: ears, eyes, whiskers and head carry every emotion. Laser focus and pinned ears while fleeing, a quick smug glance after the big dodges, shock then pure fury after the gull. The owner plays big readable physical comedy: furious, clumsy, slipping and falling, crashing into the door, leaping helplessly at the wall, then laughing; his lips move only on his four lines and his laugh. The woman reacts wide-eyed and quick, with her lips closed. Living eyes with sharp catch-lights, every hair of fur crisp and photoreal.

PHYSICS

Real mass and inertia, all motion in forward real time at high speed: the cat gallops in long powerful bounds on three legs, its spine stretching and bunching; its paws slip and scrabble on the polished wood in the turns and its body leans into every corner. The salmon fillet flops and swings in its jaws with every bound. The slipper flies in a fast flat line, spinning. The cushion and broom fly in true arcs and bounce when they land. The owner falls with real weight and slides on the wood. The cat flap swings on its hinge and slaps shut. The hops onto the bench, the wall and the roof are short, explosive cat leaps, back legs driving, claws gripping wood, stone and tile. The gull's wingbeats blow the cat's fur flat and the salmon tugs out of its teeth with a visible jerk of its head.

LIGHTING

Interior lit by bright daylight from large windows, 5600K, soft and even, normal exposure. The exterior is hard midday sun, 5600K, one stop brighter than the interior, with crisp shadows on the lawn and a bright rim light on the cat's fur.

AUDIO

Loud, punchy diegetic sound and the owner's shouts, with no music. 0.0s: a quiet kitchen and a drink being poured. At 1.0s a wet bite and a plate clink. At 1.8s a clatter as the camera is grabbed, then the thump of the cat landing. At 2.0s the owner yells: "Hey! No, no, no!" From 2.4s the cat's claws drumming fast and the owner's heavy footsteps and panting. At 3.4s the whoosh of the slipper. At 4.8s squeaking socks and a thump on the door frame. At 5.0s the owner shouts: "Come on!" At 6.8s a robotic beep, a crash and a heavy body thud. At 7.8s the whoosh of the cushion. From 9.0s the dachshund's frantic high barks, continuing to the end. At 10.9s a whoosh and a wooden clatter. At 12.4s the owner yells: "Not the flap!" At 13.6s the plastic clack of the cat flap, swinging. At 14.4s a heavy thud against the door. From 15.0s, outdoor ambience: distant waves, seagull cries, the cat's quick panting, claws on wood, stone and tile. At 16.0s the door bangs open and running footsteps cross the grass. At 18.4s the owner yells up: "Get down here!" At 20.6s a beating of wings and a loud gull screech. From 21.4s the cat's long angry yowl, the owner's laughter from below and the gull's cries overhead, the drumming of paws on tile to the last frame.

STYLE

Photoreal selfie action-cam pet footage, candid and chaotic, viral-video energy, high-speed frantic slapstick comedy with sharp, high-contrast daylight.

OUTPUT SETTINGS

Vertical 9:16, 24 seconds, real-time speed for the whole shot, smooth 60 fps motion.

From 13.6s to 16.0s the owner is inside behind the closed front door; from 16.0s he is on the lawn below the garage. From 17.4s to the end the cat is on the garage roof, 3 meters above the lawn, and the owner and the dachshund are on the lawn below, the owner's fingertips always at least 1 meter below the roof edge. entries.prompt:
Create a **15-second photorealistic video, 1080p, 60 fps**, in one continuous shot. A massive round snow boulder drops straight down from a hovering helicopter into a wide lava lake.

**The movement is a vertical free fall, exactly like dropping a heavy rock. The snow has no sideways momentum.**

**CAMERA AND ALIGNMENT**

Use a strict overhead view. The lens points vertically downward throughout the shot. The camera, snow boulder, and center of the lava lake are stacked along one vertical line.

The helicopter hovers motionless directly above the landing point. The camera descends vertically after the snow while maintaining the same horizontal position. Keep the center of the lava lake directly beneath the snow throughout the descent.

The crater expands outward around the center of the image as the camera approaches. There is no sideways scenery movement, horizon, orbit, or diagonal tracking.

**0–1 second — Drop straight down.**

A huge, approximately three-meter-wide sphere of compacted snow hangs beneath the helicopter in an external release sling. Its surface is rough, granular, and uneven. Part of the landing gear is visible at the edge of the opening frame.

Far below, a broad crater contains an exposed orange lava lake approximately 200 meters across.

The sling opens without swinging. The snow drops vertically from rest. Hold the camera briefly at its initial height so the increasing distance clearly establishes that the boulder is falling away from the helicopter.

**1–10 seconds — Vertical free fall.**

The camera accelerates straight downward after the snow, then follows approximately five to seven meters above it.

Keep the snow large and detailed in the foreground, occupying roughly one-third of the frame’s width. It falls heavily, with minimal rotation. Small loose crumbs separate from its surface.

The lava lake remains centered beneath it and grows rapidly larger. Its dark crust and glowing currents become increasingly detailed. Use a fixed focal length and continuous downward camera movement.

The snow follows the same vertical line for the entire fall. It does not glide, fly forward, swing, or correct its trajectory. The descent feels fast, heavy, and uninterrupted, with natural acceleration and motion blur.

**10–11 seconds — Direct impact.**

The camera begins slowing its downward movement while remaining directly above the snow. The boulder continues straight down, moving farther from the camera.

Show its underside striking the exposed molten surface at the exact point beneath its original release position.

**11–15 seconds — Steam and lava eruption.**

The impact displaces the lava outward. A powerful white steam plume erupts from the contact point, carrying thick orange lava sheets and heavy glowing droplets.

The snow disappears inside the blast. A circular wave spreads across the lava lake. Maintain the overhead view as steam expands toward the camera and molten fragments arc outward.

End during the eruption.

**AUDIO**

Helicopter rotors at the opening, fading as the camera descends. Strong rushing wind during the fall. A heavy impact followed by a powerful steam roar and molten splashes.

Natural daylight and realistic material textures. No cuts, slow motion, music, dialogue, captions, or logos.

Image 1 defines the man in all five shots. Match his face, tousled wavy dark-brown hair, brown eyes, light stubble, navy crew-neck T-shirt, loose taupe drawstring lounge pants and dark gray house slippers.

Image 2 defines the woman in all five shots. Match her face, green eyes, freckles, long copper-red hair in a high wavy ponytail, cream ribbed long-sleeve Henley, sage-green drawstring pants and cream house slippers. Keep her sleeves pushed up as in the photo.

Video 1 defines the kitchen, framing, camera angles, body movements, edit timing, red flames, blue glow and final embrace. Use the facial designs from the photos and the changing expressions described below. The woman's new English vocal performance determines her lip movements.

VOICE AND SOUND
Begin on the first frame with the woman already yelling directly at the man. Her voice is loud, forward and distinct above the kitchen ambience. She sounds personally hurt and furious. Her pitch rises on accusations, her consonants bite, and her voice strains slightly on stressed words. Let each phrase run straight into the next. Record the entire outburst as one continuous performance across shots 1 through 4.

This is her complete line, spoken once:
“You never listen! Every time I try to talk to you, you just stand there! Say something! Do you even understand why I'm so upse-”

She is the only speaker. During his close-up, her shouting continues offscreen at the same intensity and intelligibility. Keep it loud as he approaches and opens his arms. Cut off the final word “upset” in mid-syllable on the exact frame his arms close around her. Use one female vocal track. Preserve compatible background sound from Video 1 beneath it. After the cutoff, let the small sounds of her breath and his shirt shifting become audible.

SETTING
A home kitchen at night, rendered in the polished cinematic 3D style of the character references. Warm pendant lamps illuminate a pale countertop on a dark island. A shallow bowl rests on the counter. A dark blue window is visible behind the woman. Keep the kitchen layout consistent. Let the colored light from each character fall naturally across skin, clothing and nearby surfaces.

SHOT 1 | 0.000-1.625s
Medium two-shot. The man stands in the left foreground, seen from behind and partly in profile. Across the island, the woman leans into both palms and yells “You never listen!” straight at him. On “listen,” she lifts one hand and points sharply at him across the countertop. Her other palm stays planted to support her weight. Her ponytail swings with the gesture. Red light flares along her extended forearm. Cut with her finger still pointing and her outburst in progress.

SHOT 2 | 1.625-3.375s
Wider view on the same axis, man on the left, woman on the right. Begin with her pointing arm already extended. She sweeps it down as she drives into “Every time I try to talk to you.” Her brows pinch inward, her jaw opens wide on stressed vowels and her shoulders stay tense. Tall red flames rise behind her back and ponytail, casting moving highlights onto her cheek and cream sleeve. Her face remains clearly visible. The man holds her gaze.

SHOT 3 | 3.375-6.750s
Cut to a near-frontal close-up of the man from the upper chest. Carry her voice straight across the edit. The accusation continues from her position across the island and builds to “you just stand there! Say something!” His closed lips and steady eyeline make it clear he is listening. A warm red reflection flickers across his face. His eyelids briefly lower. When he opens them, blue light appears in his eyes and softly traces his curls and shoulders. His brow relaxes and a small, reassuring smile appears. Her shouting continues over that smile.

SHOT 4 | 6.750-10.042s
Return to the full-body wide shot. The man is on the left, outlined in blue down to his slippers. The woman is on the right, still visibly shouting. Pick up her lip movements on the syllable currently being heard. As she delivers “Do you even understand why I'm so upse-”, he walks around the camera-facing end of the island toward her. A faint blue trace follows his slippers. She turns her head to keep addressing him. The flames remain high.

He clears the corner and opens his arms. She is still yelling directly at him. Show his arms close around her upper back in the wide shot, immediately before the cut. That contact interrupts the final word. Her body is still tense and her flames are still visible as the shot ends.

SHOT 5 | 10.042-18.042s
One uninterrupted close-up over his shoulder. His navy shirt fills the lower foreground, his head is on screen right, and her face is visible just left of his head. The embrace is already in progress. He holds her steadily throughout.

10.042-11.500s. Her voice has stopped, but her brow is still furrowed and her jaw remains tense for a moment. Red flames are visible behind her ponytail. Then her green eyes widen, her jaw loosens and her lips part on a small caught breath. She registers the hug.

11.500-13.500s. Her inner brows lift. She glances down toward his shoulder. The tall flames shrink and disappear, leaving a little warmth on her cheek. By about 13.1s, her first hand rests lightly on the upper back of his shirt. Her eyes are still open. A faint blue edge is visible along his silhouette.

13.500-15.500s. She closes her eyes and settles her cheek against his shoulder. Her forearm slides farther across his back. She brings her other arm around him and her shoulders relax. Blue light catches the edges of her copper ponytail.

15.500-18.042s. She draws him closer, gently gathering the navy fabric in her fingers. A small, relieved smile forms while her cheek stays against him. Soft blue light surrounds them both. End inside the embrace.

CONTINUITY
Keep the pointing gesture continuous across the first cut and the embrace continuous across the last. The shout ends instantly at contact. The anger in her face and the red flames take several more seconds to subside. Keep her copper hair visually distinct from the flames. Maintain both photo identities, outfits, the bowl and the position of the island throughout. No subtitles, narration or end card.

entries.title: One woman, three emotions, one continuous take: happiness to crying to anger with lip-synced dialogue on a white studio background (Kling 4.0 Flash)
entries.description: A performance stress test: one locked portrait, three emotional states in sequence, with natural spoken dialogue, visible tears and microexpressions. The plain white set isolates the acting. Useful for testimonial or casting tests.
entries.prompt:
Create an ultra-photorealistic cinematic portrait video featuring one woman experiencing three powerful emotions in a continuous, uninterrupted performance: genuine happiness, heartbreaking sadness with visible crying, and explosive anger. Her emotional changes must feel psychologically believable, with natural spoken dialogue, accurate lip synchronization, subtle facial microexpressions, realistic tears, and expressive vocal delivery.

Environment: A minimalist portrait studio with a pure white background, soft diffused frontal lighting, delicate natural shadows, and no distracting objects.

Character: A woman in her early thirties with expressive brown eyes, natural facial features, softly styled dark hair, minimal makeup, and a modest black high-neck top. Her identity, hairstyle, clothing, and facial proportions remain completely consistent.

Visual Style: Ultra-photorealistic facial performance, visible skin pores, fine facial hairs, realistic muscle contractions, natural eye moisture, detailed tear formation, subtle lip trembling, authentic breathing, and physically accurate facial movement.

Camera Language: One continuous intimate close-up framing her face and shoulders. The camera performs an extremely slow forward push throughout the entire sequence, gradually moving closer to emphasize the emotional intensity. No cuts, no angle changes, no sudden camera movements.

Audio: Clear natural female dialogue with precise lip synchronization, emotional vocal changes, audible breathing, soft laughter, trembling speech, sobbing, and increasingly forceful angry delivery. No background music.

[00:00-00:06] HAPPINESS | Genuine Joy

Begin with the woman looking directly into the camera, her face relaxed and her eyes bright. A small, spontaneous smile appears at the corners of her lips, gradually spreading into a beautiful, genuine expression of happiness. Her cheeks lift, delicate smile lines develop around her eyes, and she releases a quiet, breathy laugh. Her shoulders relax as she leans almost imperceptibly toward the camera, appearing excited and emotionally overwhelmed by wonderful news.

She speaks in a warm, joyful voice, smiling naturally between words:

Dialogue: "I can't believe it... I'm so happy. This is everything I ever wanted!"

Her eyes sparkle with excitement, and she finishes the sentence with a soft laugh. Toward the end of the moment, her smile begins to weaken as an unexpected realization crosses her face.

[00:06-00:13] CRYING | Heartbreak

Her happiness gradually collapses into sadness. The smile disappears, her eyebrows lift toward the center, and her eyes begin filling with tears. She tries to maintain composure, pressing her trembling lips together while taking a shaky breath. Moisture gathers along her lower eyelids before the first tear spills over and slowly travels down her cheek.

Her breathing becomes uneven, her chin trembles, and she attempts to speak through the emotion. Her voice cracks naturally, interrupted by a small involuntary sob.

Dialogue: "But... you promised me. You said you'd never leave me..."

She struggles to finish the sentence, briefly lowering her gaze as another tear begins rolling down her opposite cheek. Her mouth trembles, her nostrils flare with a shaky inhale, and she closes her eyes momentarily as the pain becomes overwhelming. Her crying must feel authentic and restrained, with visible emotional effort rather than exaggerated theatrical sobbing.

[00:13-00:20] ANGER | Emotional Explosion

Her sadness gradually transforms into anger while the tears remain visible on her cheeks. She inhales sharply, raises her head, and fixes her eyes directly on the camera. Her eyebrows lower, her jaw tightens, and the trembling in her lips gradually becomes a firm, controlled expression. Her breathing changes from broken sobs into deeper, more forceful breaths.

She begins speaking through clenched teeth, her voice initially low and shaking with suppressed anger.

Dialogue: "You lied to me..."

She pauses briefly, swallowing her emotions as her eyes narrow and her facial muscles tense. Her voice suddenly rises with genuine fury.

Dialogue: "HOW COULD YOU DO THIS TO ME?!"

Her eyebrows pull together sharply, her nostrils flare, and her mouth opens naturally with the force of the final words. Her voice breaks slightly because she is still crying, creating a believable mixture of heartbreak and rage. She finishes the sentence breathing heavily, her jaw clenched, tears still visible, and her eyes locked intensely on the camera.

The final frame holds on her furious, tear-streaked face as she struggles to regain control.

Emotional Continuity: The performance must feel like one uninterrupted emotional experience. Happiness gradually gives way to heartbreak, and heartbreak intensifies into anger. Preserve overlapping emotional cues, particularly the transition from crying into rage, where tears continue flowing even as her facial expression becomes increasingly aggressive.

Facial Performance: Prioritize realistic facial anatomy, natural asymmetry, detailed eyebrow movement, subtle cheek tension, lower-lip trembling, involuntary blinking, eye moisture, visible tear accumulation, realistic tear trails, and physically accurate jaw movement during speech.

Dialogue and Lip Synchronization: Every spoken word must align precisely with her mouth movements. Her voice should evolve naturally from light, joyful warmth to fragile, trembling sadness and finally intense, emotionally strained anger. Include realistic pauses, breaths, vocal cracks, and changes in volume without making the dialogue sound theatrical or artificially generated.

Camera and Lighting: Maintain a single continuous close-up with a very slow push-in. Preserve identical facial proportions, hairstyle, clothing, white background, lighting direction, and skin texture throughout.

Negative Guidance: No identity changes, sudden emotional switching, exaggerated facial acting, cartoon expressions, artificial tears, frozen eyes, unnatural mouth movements, inaccurate lip synchronization, inconsistent tear positions, plastic skin, beauty filters, facial morphing, camera cuts, subtitles, text, logos, background music, or additional characters.

entries.prompt:
30-second, 4K, 16:9 ultra-realistic home video shot on an early-2000s consumer DV camcorder.

A quiet Sunday afternoon in an older Seoul residential neighborhood, filmed by a friend walking with her.

One continuous handheld recording with a couple of casual cuts, like someone pausing and restarting the tape.

SUBJECT
A young Korean woman in her early 20s, the same person in every moment.
Natural beauty, realistic skin texture, minimal makeup.
Black wavy hair in a messy side ponytail over her left shoulder.
Fitted pastel-blue short top, loose cream pajama-style pants, black sneakers, a thin simple silver necklace.
A small beige reusable canvas shopping bag hangs on her left shoulder the whole time.
Her face, hair, outfit and bag stay exactly the same throughout.

LITTLE GIRL
A Korean girl about 6 years old, short bob haircut, yellow T-shirt, denim shorts, small pink sneakers.

THE BALLOON
One round red helium balloon on a thin white string.
Only one balloon exists in the video.

LOCATION
A quiet older Seoul neighborhood on a mild sunny afternoon.
Narrow residential lane, low brick houses, red-brick villas, potted plants by doorways, parked bicycles, utility poles with tangled overhead wires, mature trees.
A small neighborhood playground with a slide, a sandbox and a few low trees along a short fence.

CAMERA & LOOK
Raw handheld early-2000s DV camcorder footage.
Shaky hand movement, autofocus hunting, faded slightly cyan-tinted colors, exposure shifts between sun and shade, motion blur, soft standard-definition-like detail upscaled, occasional accidental zoom in and out, imperfect off-center framing.
The camera operator sometimes reacts a little late.

AUDIO
Natural neighborhood ambience recorded by the camcorder mic: birds, children playing in the distance, a bicycle bell, footsteps on asphalt, wind hitting the mic, faint distant traffic.
No music.

0–5s — LANE
She walks slowly through the quiet residential lane, shopping bag on her left shoulder, the camera following slightly behind and to her right.
Sunlight flickers through the trees.

5–10s — PLAYGROUND
She passes the small playground.
The camera accidentally zooms in and finds the little girl on tiptoe under a low tree branch, reaching up but unable to touch the red balloon caught in the leaves, its string dangling just out of reach.
The woman slows down, notices her, and walks over.

10–17s — FREEING THE BALLOON
Medium shot from the side.
Standing beside the girl, the woman reaches up with her right hand, gently untangles the string from the branch and pulls the red balloon down.
The string is clearly held in her right hand.
She bends down and places the string into the girl's small hand; the girl grips it tightly and the balloon floats above her head.

17–21s — THANK YOU
Same continuous shot, both of them in frame, the camera slightly off to the side.
The girl looks up holding the balloon and says brightly in English: "Thank you!"
The woman smiles and replies softly: "You're welcome."
The girl runs back toward the slide, still holding the balloon string, the red balloon bobbing above her.

21–26s — WALKING HOME
Cut.
The woman walks on down the lane, smiling to herself, bag on her left shoulder.
A light breeze moves loose strands of her hair, and a few dry leaves skitter across the street.
The camera follows a few steps behind, wobbling.

26–30s — HOME
She reaches the gate of a small red-brick house, opens it, then turns back toward the camera and says with a relaxed smile: "Pretty nice Sunday."
She steps inside and the gate swings shut.
Hard cut to black.

- SOUND DESIGN: Heavy glass-on-marble placement, sharp fingernail glass taps, magnetic lid snap, foil seal peel-pop, soft creamy spatula glide, skin-on-skin massage swipes, skin press suction-pat, final magnetic closure snap.

00:12 - 00:16 | SPATULA SCOOP & TEXTURE LIFT

- ACTION: Elena glides the sleek metallic spatula through the top layer of cream, lifting a thick, velvety dollop of whipped cream and holding it steady under warm key light.

Reference: 程远＝一名三十二岁上下的东亚男性，短黑发微乱，穿深灰羊毛大衣配黑色高领毛衣；林夏＝一名三十岁上下的东亚女性，低马尾，穿米白风衣；全片两人面部、发型、体型与穿着完全一致。
Audio: 深夜咖啡馆低沉的冰箱嗡鸣、窗外淅沥雨声、陶瓷杯轻碰碟子的脆响、衣料摩擦声；现场中文对白（台词见节拍内），口型与台词严格同步；无旁白、无音乐、无字幕
Overall style: 8K IMAX 超写实电影，Lubezki×Deakins 摄影，只用场景内实际光源，毛孔级皮肤，180°快门运动模糊，物理重量真实，拒绝游戏CG感

GLOBAL CONTINUITY
Setting:
深夜临街小咖啡馆靠窗卡座，深胡桃木桌面有两只白瓷咖啡杯与一张折成两半的登机牌；左侧是挂满雨珠的整面落地玻璃窗，窗外是模糊的城市湿漉街景与暖黄路灯。
Main subject:
程远与林夏为双主角，身份、面部与服装全程一致。
Props:
白色纸质登机牌折成两半，平放在深胡桃木桌面正中央，距程远右手约 15 厘米。
Blocking:
程远坐画左面朝画右，林夏坐画右面朝画左，两人隔着宽约 0.9 米的木桌正对而坐，互不遮挡。
Lighting:
室内主灯关闭，仅靠桌面正上方一盏低垂暖钨丝吊灯（2800K）照亮桌面与两人半侧脸，窗外街灯冷蓝反光轻擦两人肩背。摄影机始终在人物阴影侧，无任何外部补光。
Color:
60:30:10——深棕暗影 / 暖钨丝琥珀 / 窗外冷蓝反光点缀

CAMERA CONTINUITY
全片严格只有 2 次硬切，分别在第 7.0 秒和第 14.0 秒，无过渡、无淡入淡出。前两段采用极轻的手持呼吸感 (Subtle handheld shake)，最后一段切为几乎察觉不到的缓慢推近 (Slow push-in / Dolly in)。

PERFORMANCE ENGINE
程远｜目的：把登机牌推回给林夏劝她别走 障碍：说出口就等于承认自己输了 隐藏的恐惧：她真的会头也不回 保护策略：用故作轻松的慢动作掩盖手抖
林夏｜目的：等程远亲口说一句留下来 障碍：尊严不允许先低头 隐藏的恐惧：他只是客套 保护策略：压低视线盯住杯口不接话
情绪曲线：控制 → 加压 → 裂缝 → 暴露 → 残留

0.0–7.0秒｜推牌试探
镜头开场即在运动中，程远右手食指和中指压在桌面登机牌边缘，把登机牌顺着木纹慢慢往林夏那边推过 10 厘米后手指停住；林夏左手握着白瓷杯柄，拇指在杯沿轻轻摩挲半圈，眼睛盯着桌面没抬头。
7.0–14.0秒｜硬切对峙与开口
第 7.0 秒动量匹配硬切 (Match cut) 至林夏半身胸像 (Medium close-up / Bust shot)。林夏听见纸张摩擦桌面的声音停下，先轻吸一口气，才慢慢抬眼直视画左的程远，嘴角先扯出一丝极淡的苦笑，随后笑意从眼里退掉，开口说出台词。
14.0–20.0秒｜反打破防与残留
第 14.0 秒同轴反打硬切 (Cut on axis) 至程远面部特写 (Close-up)。程远原本紧绷的下颌微微一松，喉结上下滚动一次，眼眶迅速泛湿泛光但不落泪，右手手指无意识把登机牌边角轻轻压平，低声接上一句台词，说完没有移开视线，停在沉默呼吸里。

Performance:
①（7.0–14.0秒）触发：登机牌停在杯边 → 面部：眉毛内侧极轻微抬起，下唇抿一下再松开 → 目光：从杯口缓缓抬至画左锁死对方 → 呼吸：轻吸气后平稳吐字 → 结束状态：眼神发亮但嘴角归于平直。
台词：「你每次都这样，把选择推给我。」（朝画左程远说，语速偏慢、声音轻而克制，在“这样”后停顿 0.5 秒，嘴型必须和“你-每-次-都-这-样-把-选-择-推-给-我”每个字的发音完全对上）
②（14.0–20.0秒）触发：听完林夏的话 → 面部：咬肌松开、眼皮微颤、眼球泛水光但眼泪不得早于第 20.0 秒落下 → 呼吸：鼻腔短促吸气一次 → 结束状态：嘴唇闭合，胸口缓慢起伏。
台词：「这次是我不敢留你。」（朝画右林夏说，音量压低、尾音略带气声，嘴型必须和“这-次-是-我-不-敢-留-你”每个字的发音完全对上）

Environment:
窗外雨滴沿玻璃缓慢滑落，远处偶尔有一辆车尾灯的红光在湿漉玻璃上拉出模糊光斑，咖啡馆内其余座位空无一人。
Camera:
0.0–7.0秒 35mm 双人侧景 (Two-shot) 手持呼吸感极缓横移 → 7.0秒硬切 50mm 林夏过肩半身胸像 (Medium close-up / Bust shot) 稳住焦平面 → 14.0秒硬切 85mm F1.4 程远面部特写 (Close-up) 极缓慢推近 (Slow push-in / Dolly in) 约 6 厘米。
Constraints:
登机牌始终留在桌面两人之间，不得凭空消失或变成其他纸张；两人的左右站位轴线全程锁死；口型与台词逐字严格同步，说完立刻闭唇。

---
Negative:
改变程远和林夏人物造型，重新设计服装，服装漂移，面部漂移，人物替换
多余切镜，机位瞬移，越轴，场景跳变，变焦推拉
静止发呆开场，表情一步到位，开场就崩溃，提前流泪，夸张肢体动作
登机牌消失，咖啡杯位置跳变，多手多指，口型与中文台词错位
动漫渲染，游戏CG，塑料皮肤，过度磨皮，正面补光，反光板，柔光箱

entries.prompt:
ZAZA! — THE REALITY PRANK | 30-SECOND CINEMATIC MUSIC VIDEO

CHARACTER REFERENCE & IDENTITY LOCK

REFERENCE: <<<image_1>>> defines ONLY the female character's face and facial identity. Preserve her exact facial proportions, eyes, nose, lips, skin tone, and hairstyle. Her face must remain identical across ALL shots.

Do NOT use <<<image_1>>>  to determine her wardrobe.

FEMALE CHARACTER — EXACT WARDROBE DESCRIPTION:

She wears the following outfit throughout the entire video:

1. JACKET: An oversized retro 80s color-block windbreaker with a distinctive geometric design. High bright hot-pink collar, deep purple shoulders and upper sleeves, vivid hot-pink upper chest panels, large mint/turquoise lower panels, bold sunshine-yellow horizontal stripes across the chest and sleeves, mint-green triangular collar accents, and a contrasting white front zipper. Elasticated cuffs and hem, lightweight sporty fabric, relaxed oversized fit. Reproduce the exact color placement and geometric pattern described here.
2. INNERWEAR: Plain white T-shirt.
3. PANTS: Oversized cobalt-blue cargo pants with a relaxed streetwear silhouette.
4. SHOES: Colorful multicolor sneakers.
5. BAG: Black crossbody shoulder bag.

CRITICAL WARDROBE LOCK: The pink, purple, turquoise, and yellow windbreaker must remain exactly the same in every scene. Never replace it with a teal/orange jacket. No redesign, no color changes, no missing stripes, no altered geometric panels, no wardrobe drift. Maintain the same clothing, hairstyle, face, and body proportions throughout the entire video.

---

VISUAL STYLE

Premium editorial cinematic film, surreal elastic architecture, giant glossy 3D letters spelling ZAZA!, kinetic graphic panels, bold hot pink, turquoise, electric lime, cobalt, orange, violet, sunshine yellow, and warm ivory.

High-end commercial production quality. Beautiful cinematic lighting, realistic skin texture, natural facial expressions, realistic human movement, authentic fabric physics, and highly detailed CGI environments.

Real human character, surreal CGI objects and architecture. One coherent city/studio world.

MUSIC & VOCALS

Original 132 BPM electro-funk / nu-disco, 4/4.

Music includes slap bass, punchy drums, bright synth brass, rhythmic guitar, hand claps, playful elastic boings, and energetic electronic accents.

Playful, youthful female singing voice with a confident, cheeky, expressive personality.

English lyrics ONLY, except the signature exclamation "ZA-ZA!"

The exact lyrics and their order must follow the timeline below. Do not add, remove, duplicate, or rearrange lyrics.

Lip-sync only when the character visibly speaks. Otherwise, use the female singing voice as background vocals.

The character reacts naturally to every musical accent, vocal trigger, and sound effect.

---

SCENE-BY-SCENE STORYBOARD

00:00–00:04 | EYE HOOK

LYRIC: "Psst, look alive... ZA-ZA!"

Extreme close-up of her eyes with a mischievous half-smile.

Precisely ON the words "ZA-ZA!", the camera CRASH-PULLS BACK to reveal an entire city street folding upward like hinged pop-up architecture.

Buildings transform AFTER the vocal trigger, never before.

Smooth depth parallax, dramatic perspective, and elastic architectural movement.

00:04–00:09 | PIANO STREET

LYRIC: "One step left, watch the street unfold!"

She confidently strides forward.

The crosswalk stripes rise into colorful elastic piano keys ONLY where her sneakers land.

Each step naturally depresses a key and triggers a musical note.

Realistic foot contact, believable walking motion, and synchronized musical reactions.

Foot-level tracking follows her steps, then a fast whip-tilt reveals the transformed street.

00:09–00:14 | CHASE THE Z

LYRIC: "Catch that Z — too fast to hold!"

A huge glossy electric-lime 3D letter Z floats near her face.

She reaches toward it with her right hand.

The Z dodges to HER RIGHT and slips behind her shoulder.

She turns in surprise and playfully chases it.

Over-shoulder push-in → rapid lateral chase → camera passes through the open negative space around the Z for a motivated visual transition.

Keep the object movement, character eyeline, and camera direction perfectly connected.

00:14–00:20 | FASHION GROOVE

LYRIC: "Blue and orange, watch me move! ZA-ZA! Hey, feel the groove!"

She performs an energetic fashion runway walk with a confident shoulder roll, playful head tilt, stylish body movement, and a clean turn toward the camera.

Her exact pink, purple, turquoise, and yellow jacket remains unchanged and clearly visible.

Architectural panels switch colors with every footstep.

Fast side tracking → low-angle push-in → rising overhead reveal → snap back to front on "ZA-ZA!"

Giant glossy ZAZA! letters assemble in the distance behind her.

00:20–00:24 | REVERSE PRANK

LYRIC: "Oops! That bounce is coming through!"

A giant orange 3D exclamation mark springs from screen-left toward her.

She playfully reaches out to grab it but misses.

It rebounds behind her shoulder and surprises her.

She reacts with a funny, natural startled expression.

Maintain realistic spring physics, connected object movement, and accurate eyeline.

Camera follows its arc 120°, then dodges as the object wipes past the lens.

00:24–00:27 | EMPTY WORLD

LYRIC: "Wait... where did the whole world go?"

The beat briefly thins to a soft bass pulse.

Buildings, giant letters, and architectural panels collapse inward and vanish, leaving a completely clean warm-ivory space.

She quickly glances left and right with a confused, funny expression.

Fast pullback → short push-in.

No prolonged silence. Keep the musical rhythm alive.

00:27–00:30 | THE WORLD PRANKS BACK

LYRIC: "ZA-ZA! Ha! You got me too!"

A tiny floating ZAZA! suddenly appears behind her shoulder and chirps "ZA-ZA!"

She spins around, flinches in surprise, then gives an embarrassed laugh.

Camera snaps from close-up to wide, revealing a GIANT glossy 3D ZAZA! logo.

The logo bounces ONCE on the final funk hit.

End exactly at 30 seconds.

---

CAMERA & MOTION DIRECTION

Every camera movement must be motivated by the female character or a transforming object.

Use:

- Dramatic close-ups and extreme close-ups.
- Fast tracking shots.
- Dynamic push-ins and pullbacks.
- Whip-pan transitions.
- Foreground object occlusion.
- Cinematic parallax and perspective.
- Dramatic scale changes.
- Smooth transitions between wide and close shots.
- Natural character movement and expressive reactions.

Maintain consistent motion direction and spatial continuity.

No random camera orbits, no disconnected movements, no stationary montage.

Musical edits must synchronize with character actions, object movements, and sound effects.

No dead air.

---

NEGATIVE PROMPT — STRICT RULES

- No face or identity drift.
- No hairstyle changes.
- No wardrobe changes.
- No replacement jacket.
- No teal/orange/cobalt jacket.
- No missing pink, purple, turquoise, or yellow jacket panels.
- No altered jacket geometry.
- No extra hero characters.
- No distorted hands or fingers.
- No incorrect Z dodge direction.
- No disconnected footwork.
- No teleporting camera.
- No random transformations.
- No misspelled ZAZA!
- No unwanted text or subtitles.
- No logo artifacts.
- No watermarks.
- No flat CGI human.
- No unrelated props.
- No duplicate lyrics.
- No altered lyric order.
- No missing final prank.
- No fade to black.

FINAL BRAND CONSISTENCY RULE

The ONLY signature catchphrase is ZA-ZA!

The giant final logo must spell ZAZA! exactly.

The female character must retain the same face, hairstyle, body proportions, and complete pink/purple/turquoise/yellow windbreaker outfit throughout all seven scenes.

FINAL RESULT: A premium, playful, visually spectacular 30-second female-led electro-funk fashion prank commercial with a memorable ZAZA! identity.

entries.prompt:
Create a 30-second, 1080p ultra-realistic personal home-video showing an ordinary summer evening in the life of a young Korean woman. No reference image.

MAIN SUBJECT

Young Korean woman in her early 20s, naturally pretty, realistic skin texture, minimal makeup, relaxed and approachable personality.

Long black hair loosely tied into a messy side ponytail with a few loose strands around her face. Wearing a fitted pastel-blue short top, loose cream pajama-style pants, black sneakers and a simple silver necklace.

Maintain the same face, hairstyle, clothing, body proportions and overall appearance throughout the entire video.

SETTING

A quiet older Seoul residential neighborhood during a warm summer evening. Narrow concrete lanes, small houses, potted plants, bicycles, old walls, utility poles, overhead wires, a tiny neighborhood bakery, a public water tap and large leafy trees casting shadows across the street.

Everything should feel lived-in, ordinary and peaceful. No tourist attractions, advertisements, recognizable brands or commercial activity.

CAMERA / VISUAL AESTHETIC

Raw personal footage casually recorded by a friend on an early-2000s consumer DV camcorder.

Strong handheld shake, imperfect framing, autofocus hunting, exposure shifts, occasional motion blur, faded colors, soft digital detail, mild noise, accidental zooms and natural camera imperfections.

No stabilization, drone footage, gimbal movement, dramatic lighting or polished commercial cinematography.

 — OUTSIDE THE HOUSE

She steps outside carrying a small reusable shopping bag. She locks the door, adjusts her messy ponytail and looks toward the camera with a relaxed smile.

A light summer breeze moves her hair as she starts walking down the lane.

 — BAKERY STOP

She reaches a tiny neighborhood bakery and buys a warm pastry.

She steps outside, takes her first bite and immediately smiles because it tastes good.

She notices her friend filming and holds the pastry toward the camera playfully before taking another bite.

— WALKING HOME

She continues down the narrow street while eating.

A neighborhood cat follows her for a few steps. She notices it, crouches down and gently pets it.

The cat walks away and she laughs before continuing.

 — SMALL ACCIDENT

She walks beneath a large tree when a few leaves fall onto her hair.

She stops, looks confused, then realizes what happened and laughs.

She brushes the leaves away while her friend zooms awkwardly toward her face.

She looks directly into the camera and says:

"Seriously?"

 — QUIET MOMENT

She reaches a low concrete wall beside the street and sits down for a moment.

She finishes the pastry while watching bicycles and neighbors passing through the lane.

A gentle breeze moves her hair. She casually fixes her ponytail and looks around peacefully.

 — FINAL MOMENT

She stands up and continues walking home.

After a few steps, she turns back toward the camera with a small playful smile and says:

"Come on."

She keeps walking down the sunny lane while the camera follows behind.

She disappears around the corner and the recording abruptly cuts to black.

AUDIO

Natural location sound only: birds, summer insects, footsteps, bicycle bells, distant scooters, leaves moving in the breeze, bakery sounds, neighborhood conversations and subtle camera-handling noise.

No music. No narration. No artificial sound effects.

Only the two spoken lines specified above.

FINAL FEEL

The entire video should feel like a forgotten summer recording from the early 2000s.

Warm, feminine, casual, slightly playful, intimate and nostalgic.

No dramatic events, no exaggerated acting, no model poses and no polished cinematic shots.

sections.title: Status & capabilities

items.text: Seedance 2.5 is real and official. ByteDance Seed launched it on 2026-07-31 on Jimeng AI (Dreamina) and Doubao Pro, with API access via BytePlus ModelArk.
One generation runs up to 30 seconds with joint audio and video (Seedance 2.0 maxed out at 15 s). Clips can be extended over multiple rounds; the project page says "extend twice".

A single request takes up to 50 reference assets: up to 30 images (up to 4K), 10 videos and 10 audio clips. Total video and total audio length are each capped at 30 s. (Seedance 2.5 only; Seedance 2.5 flash takes up to 10 images, 5 videos and 5 audio clips, per the official docs updated 2026-11-15.)

Other headline features: stronger instruction following, timestamp-level editing, extension, 3D clay-model ("white model") rendering, green-screen editing, and native speech in more than 10 languages.
ByteDance offers an official prompt-optimizer skill: install the "sd25-pe" skill, then type "/sd25-pe + your prompt".

Seedance 2.5 flash (dreamina-seedance-2-5-flash-261115) is live on the BytePlus API since 2026-11-14, 10:00 PM PT: same task types, prompt guide and 4–30 s range as Seedance 2.5, but 480p/720p only, no Draft mode, fewer references (10/5/5) and about one third cheaper per token. See "2026-11-15 additions".

Seedance 2.5 now outputs 4K (10-bit, H.265) on the BytePlus API, per the official tutorial updated 2026-11-16, including Draft → 4K finals; 4K is limited to 15 requests per minute and 1 concurrent task. Seedance 2.5 flash stays at 480p/720p. See "2026-11-16 additions".

Runway added 4K output for Seedance 2.5 on 2026-11-17 (100 credits/s vs 68 at 1080p). Volcano Ark's official 4K price example is about ¥30 for 5 s 16:9 (1080p ≈ ¥18.7, 480p Draft ≈ ¥3.4). Draft mode exists only on Seedance 2.5. See "2026-11-17 additions".

New official skill (2026-11-18): seed-audio-1-5-pe, a SeedAudio 1.5 prompt optimizer that turns Seedance prompts into sound-only scripts (6-minute audio, 6 audio refs + 1 video ref, provisional). Seedance 2.5 docs unchanged. See "2026-11-18 additions".

Faces (official, newly covered 2026-11-19): real-face uploads are rejected; use preset digital characters (asset://), your own trusted outputs from the last 30 days, or authorized real-person assets, and call them "Image 1", "Image 2" in the prompt. Seedance 2.5 prompt docs unchanged. See "2026-11-19 additions".
Reference videos (official, 2026-11-20): Seedance 2.5 input videos may now be up to 4096 × 2160 total pixels (2.0 stays at 3326 × 2494). Prompt docs unchanged. See "2026-11-20 additions".

sections.title: API parameters: duration, resolution, aspect ratio

items.text: Duration is an integer from 4 to 30 s, or -1 to let the model choose.

Resolution is 480p, 720p or 1080p. Exact 2.5 sizes include 1280×720 (16:9, 720p) and 1080×1920 (9:16, 1080p). Since 2026-11-16 Seedance 2.5 also accepts 4k (e.g. 3840×2160 at 16:9, 3326×2494 at 4:3; 10-bit H.265); Seedance 2.5 flash is limited to 480p / 720p.
Ratio is one of 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, 9:16, 21:9 or adaptive (the default). First-frame, first+last-frame, edit and extend tasks only accept adaptive.
Seedance 2.5 can output any aspect ratio between 0.4 and 2.5 when you drive it with the input assets. Seedance 2.0 had only six fixed ratios.
generate_audio defaults to true. Set it to false for silent output. output_format can be mp4 or mov; mov is recommended for edit and extend to keep color, brightness and audio consistent.
omni_reference_task_type (auto / reference / edit / extend) hints which task type you want.

sections.title: Prompt structure & order (official)

items.text: Treat the model like a visual content producer and write structured prompts in this order. (1) Asset referencing: list each image, video and audio by upload number and say what it is for. (2) One-sentence summary: Subject + Location + Event + Genre/Style + Camera movement. (3) Detailed plot: a timeline or "Shot N" segments, each with visuals, camera, action, dialogue and SFX. (4) Additional notes on what must stay consistent: camera angle, environment, sound, atmosphere.
Describe things positively. Negative constraints are officially supported for subtitles and audio ("No subtitles", "No BGM; generate only environmental sounds and action sounds", "No audio").

Business workflow tips: write the 30-second story skeleton first (opening → progression → turn → ending), group references by role, use time-based sections, treat the first pass as a structure pass, and state the business goal (ad, product demo, previs) up front.

sections.title: Multi-shot, cuts & timestamps

items.text: Break the video into segments with timestamps or "Shot N". Seedance 2.5 understands integer-second timestamps; Seedance 2.0 only understands shot numbers.

Accepted timing formats: intervals ("0-3 seconds…3-7 seconds…", "[1s-4s]…[4s-8s]"), time points ("At the 2-second mark…") and relative times ("After 3 seconds…", "the frame freezes for 1 second after…").

Leave no gaps in the timeline (avoid "0-3s… 5-6s"). If a segment has too little in it, the model improvises; if it has too much, you get extra cuts or dropped beats. Don't use timestamps for high-frequency actions.
For transitions, give both the trigger point and the method, e.g. "At the 5-second mark, the camera quickly transitions leftward using a left wipe combined with a natural dissolve."

For a one-take, say so at the top. ByteDance's own examples begin "One-take handheld gimbal tracking shot…" or "single continuous take, smooth camera movement, no cuts." Body or flag occlusion can carry the camera from one subject to the next.

sections.title: Camera-move language

items.text: Plain terms work as-is: shot sizes (extreme wide → close-up), moves (push in, pull out, pan, track, follow, orbit, dive, tilt up, handheld shake), angles (low angle, overhead, first-person).
Named techniques also work directly: one-shot/long take, Hitchcock zoom/dolly zoom, aerial, FPV, bullet time, handheld, speed ramp.
For niche terms, write the term plus what it looks like: "Rack focus: the focus shifts smoothly; the foreground trees blur while the character in the background becomes clear."

You can re-plan the camera in post: edit an existing clip and change only the camera, e.g. "Keep the characters, actions, and visual style unchanged. Adjust only the camera movement. 0–4s micro-FPV… 4–7s push in and track laterally…".

Clay-model (white-model) references let you block camera, trajectory and lighting in rough 3D and have Seedance render it. Simple, coarse primitives work best. State which properties to copy ("Refer to the camera movement and motion in [Video 1]…").

sections.title: Reference images, first/last frame, keyframes & storyboards

items.text: Number assets in upload order (Image 1 / Video 1 / Audio 1) and bind every one in the prompt text, e.g. "Images 1-2 are Character 1 and correspond to Audio 1." Don't rely on names written inside the image; that causes characters to get confused or duplicated.
Upload subject references in the order each subject first appears. This fixes swapped characters.
Recommended counts: 1-8 image-referenced subjects (9-12 is less stable); 1-5 subjects for audio/video references, with 5-10 s clips.

First/last frame: setting the role to first_frame/last_frame locks the aspect ratio to the image, and both frames should share a ratio. Alternatively, use reference_image and write "Image 3 is the first frame, and Image 5 is the last frame." This doesn't lock the ratio, but the match is looser.

For strict shot-by-shot control, upload each frame as its own image and open the prompt with "Use Images X to X in order as keyframes." Multi-panel storyboards are only a loose plot reference: keep them to 15 panels or fewer, use line art, and put no text on the panels.
If a reference is already accurate, say "strictly refer to…" and don't re-describe it.

sections.title: Motion, performance, dialogue & audio

items.text: Describe actions in general terms ("several sets of high-knee raises and somersaults") and add specifics only for a few memorable beats, without repeating them. Write expressions as descriptive sentences and avoid idioms.
Audio and video are generated together: dialogue, SFX and music. Gateway docs say to put dialogue in double quotes. ByteDance's examples use {curly braces} or quotes after "X says:".
To give each line its own delivery without triggering burned-in subtitles, write: Character's line (emotion): "content". Don't repeat dialogue words elsewhere in the prompt.
You can bind a voice: "Image 1 depicts the protagonist and uses the voice timbre from Audio 1." Audio references can drive rhythm and lip-sync.

sections.title: Editing & extension (locked tasks)

items.text: Edit triggers: "edit video, add, insert, remove, delete, modify, replace, change to". The output keeps the source ratio (ratio=adaptive, duration=-1). Describe the change as A → B and use timestamps for partial edits.
Extend triggers: "extend forward, extend backward, continue, continue from, extend the story". The ratio is locked to the source and the duration is up to you.
Edited output can come out about 0.33 s short. Fix it by switching to Reference mode with a set duration, or trim the input to 8n+1 frames.

sections.title: Known failure modes → fixes (official FAQ)

items.text: The look differs from Seedance 2.0. To keep the 2.0 look, extend a 2.0 clip in 2.5 and output MOV.
Glowing eyes on strong emotion: add "normal human eyes; no glowing eyes" and swap words like "fanatical" for "amazed".
Wrong character ↔ reference mapping: reorder uploads to match first appearance and renumber the prompt.
Misspelled on-screen text: have the letters appear one by one ("D", "I", "H"…), or supply the exact text as a reference image.
Subtitles appear anyway: use the line (emotion): format, don't repeat dialogue, and use subtitle-free reference videos.
Music appears despite "No BGM": list every synonym (music, BGM, score, instrumental, melody, synth, ambient pad…) and repeat the audio rule at the start and end, or strip it in post.
Fingerprint-like textures in grass or foliage: downscale reference images to no larger than the output resolution.
Bubbling or echo audio artifacts: remove water, wave and echo instructions.
Unstable results on complex combined tasks: split into separate Reference and Edit passes. Ratio changes are more stable in Reference mode with a detailed timeline.
ByteDance admits the physics of complex motion and multi-subject interaction still need work.

sections.title: 2026-10-18 additions: official task types & FAQ details

items.text: Seamless video transition: upload two clips and have Seedance generate only the bridge between them. Official wording: "Seamlessly connect [Video 1] and [Video 2]…", plus "Do not alter the two uploaded videos themselves." Library example: TRN-023.
One-click video creation: supply only images and a short brief, and let the model write the shots. Official example: the doodle-puppy vlog (AES-024).

"Audio policy (applies to all shots)" block: put the no-music rule once at the top, list every music synonym, and repeat it inside each shot. In the official before/after (MOO-024), BGM leakage stops.
Audio translation / re-dub: give each character's complete line in the target language with a timeline, ask for word-level lip-sync, and state acceptance criteria.
Changing aspect ratio is more stable in Reference mode with a detailed [Visual timeline] than as an Edit.
An HTTP 400 on a valid-looking JPG is a non-standard encoding. Re-save with `ffmpeg -i in.jpg -pix_fmt yuvj420p fixed.jpg`, or convert to PNG.
Multi-view character sheets help with a few subjects. With more than 5 subjects, single-view images are more stable.
Edit inputs: keep source videos to 20 s or less. For edit-with-reference-images, 1-5 images is the recommended range.
Extension: the volume and loudness jump at the seam is smaller when the source was itself generated by Seedance 2.5.
Fine clay (white-model) references: remove trajectory lines, axes, gizmos and camera cones before export, or they may render into the shot.

sections.title: 2026-10-18 additions: Runway's Seedance 2.5 implementation

items.text: On Runway: 4-30 s or Auto duration; Auto, 21:9, 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4 or 9:16 ratios; MP4/MOV inputs.
Draft mode renders a cheap 480p preview that can be enhanced to 1080p within 7 days. Use it for structure passes.
Sketch edit: draw on a frame, and the sketch is passed as "@Image 1 at ss:SS". Refer to it by that timestamp.
Runway extensions return only the new footage, so stitch it to the source yourself.
Scope each reference: say what it defines and what to ignore, e.g. "Use @Image 2 only for the shoe design. Ignore its environment entirely."
Add an "End state:" line to each shot so the next shot starts from a known frame. Runway's product-film example (PRP-030) does this for every shot.
For reveals, explicitly withhold the frame: "Keep the framing low so nothing above the mist is visible" (MOO-025), then release it in the next beat.

sections.title: 2026-10-19 additions: remaining official examples, locked parameters, community patterns

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-19: the BytePlus guide is still the 2026-10-16 version, and Runway's "Creating with Seedance 2.5" article is unchanged (updated 2026-10-13). No new official Seedance 2.5 docs were found. The items below come from parts of those pages not ingested before.

"Glowing eyes" fix (official before/after): vague emotion words made the model draw literal glowing eyes. The fix writes [Video constraints] / [Setting] / [Characters] (relative heights) / [Blocking], then locked-off MCU shots where each emotion is a concrete micro-expression ("eyes widen instantly… hands tremble slightly", "slowly lowers his eyes"). Library: PRF-030.

Role-mismatch fix (official): when faces swap between characters, bind every image to a named character in one [Reference assets] line before the shots. Then make every shot restate composition, shot size, angle, interior/exterior and time, camera, location and who speaks, with dialogue in {}. Library: REA-027 (8 shots in 13 s).

Aspect-ratio change (official, Reference mode): "Create a new video using @Video 1 as the strict visual and temporal reference. Follow the output dimensions and duration selected in the generation settings." Then four blocks: [Timeline fidelity: Highest priority] (every shot, flash frame and whip pan kept at its source moment), [Reference content], [Additional canvas] (seamless outpaint of the new area, static details fixed in world space) and a per-second [Visual timeline]. Library: CAM-083 (16:9 → 9:16).

Audio translation (official): one instruction line, then 8 numbered core requirements: replace every utterance, map voices to the right characters, keep timing, emotion and volume, re-sync lips word by word, no subtitles, change nothing else, the source video wins if the timeline differs, and review segment by segment. Then a timestamped line table in {} and a "Final acceptance criteria" sentence. Library: PRF-031.

Locked parameters (re-read from the official table; today's adapted templates now follow it): editing sets ratio = adaptive and duration = -1, and recommends output_format = mov. First frame or first/last frame sets ratio = adaptive, so give both frames the same aspect ratio or the last frame is stretched. Extension sets ratio = adaptive and needs a trigger word ("extend forward/backward", "continue").

Runway's Seedance 2.0 article (updated 2026-10-15) shows how short reference prompts can be, all lowercase: "relight Video 1 to dusk with a purple sky. colorize Video 1", "apply the camera motion from Video 1 to the scene in Image 1", "use Image 1 as a storyboard to guide the scenes". All six examples are ingested (CAM-084, CAM-085, MOO-027, AES-029, PRF-032, PRP-032). For 2.5, use them as the asset-binding line and add the timeline.

Community, second-hand and unverified: a summary of Dan Kieft's Seedance 2.5 talk gives a "CTLT" checklist (Camera = lens and angle, Tone = mood, Lighting = direction and feel, Texture = pores, dust, surface). It also advises copying real operators' mistakes: shaky hands, jerky zooms, jumping exposure, drifting focus.

Operator-delay realism: "The camera tilts up with a slight delay, as a real person's would", then "The camera shakes slightly and refocuses", inside a 30 s phone one-take with mild auto-exposure shifts. Library: REA-030.

Name the device for grain: "cheap early-2000s consumer camcorder with a fisheye lens: strong barrel distortion, harsh on-camera flash" plus "raw camcorder mic audio, clipping and distorted". Library: GRN-025.
Seedance 2.0 Mini is an official, cheaper and faster sibling on Dreamina (and Volcengine). Creators label CapCut posts with it (AES-033), so don't read "2.0 Mini" results as 2.5 behavior.

Cross-model check: the new official Kling 4.0, MiniMax H3 and Wan 3.0 guides use the same skeleton as Seedance 2.5 (asset roles → global style → timed shots → audio → constraints), so their official examples (added today) port cleanly. Each has a Seedance 2.5 adapted template. One exception: Wan 3.0's red-line path drawing is not documented for Seedance, so CAM-089's adaptation describes the waypoints in words.

sections.title: 2026-10-20 additions: reference scoping, pacing, camcorder realism, cross-model ports

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-20 (about 6 AM PT): the BytePlus guide is still the 2026-10-16 version (the .md copy is byte-identical to 10-18/10-19). Runway's "Creating with Seedance 2.5" (updated 2026-10-13) and "Creating with Seedance 2.0" (updated 2026-10-15) articles are unchanged, and no new Runway Seedance article appeared. No new official Seedance 2.5 guidance today; everything below is community practice or cross-model, labelled as such.

Omni-reference role scoping (community; fits the official one-line asset binding): give each asset one job and say what it must not contribute. "@Image1 is the first frame … @Image2 is the driver: use this person's face … in Shot 2. Do not use the face of the man from @Video1. @Video1 is the reference for everything else after Shot 1 … Keep them exactly as in @Video1." Upload order is start frame → face photo → video; settings 13 s, 3:4 or 9:16, 720p, sound on. Library: TRN-032.

Timeline override (community, not in the official docs): "Ignore the timing and the order of shots in @Video1, follow the timeline below." This lets a reference video supply set, car, angles and motion while your own 4-shot timeline (0-2 / 2-5 / 5-7 / 7-13 s) sets the edit. It also puts the sound cue for each shot inline in angle brackets: "<phone buzz, notification chime>". Library: TRN-032. The official aspect-ratio example does the opposite ("[Timeline fidelity: Highest priority]", CAM-083), so pick one stance per prompt.

Pacing through mixed shot lengths (community): 8 scenes timed from 1.5 s to 3.5 s across 20 s, plus "alternating quick editorial cuts with longer character-focused moments … Clean instantaneous hard cuts only." The same prompt specifies its lower-third title down to the pixel (font and weight, 42px at 1080p, #FFFFFF on #17212B at 60% opacity, bottom-centre safe area, about 2 s, "Never render floating white text or position it at the top"). Library: TRN-033.

Camcorder realism keeps converging on operator behaviour, not filters: "The camera behaves like a friend casually filming them, sometimes reacting late or briefly losing the action" (GRN-027). In UGC: "natural autofocus breathing, handheld imperfections, fast jump cuts" plus negatives "cinematic grading, commercial production … perfect stabilization" (PRP-034). The same recipe works on MiniMax H3 ("The camera operator misses part of the first step, then quickly reframes", GRN-028).

Long briefs vs the 30 s cap: one creator's 60 s, 8-shot brief (a REFERENCE LOCK list @[ref1]…@[ref5], a rule-based plot, and FINAL RULES for continuity) was posted as a ~15 s video. Seedance 2.5 caps a single generation at 30 s, so split anything longer into ≤30 s generations or extensions and repeat the lock list in each. Library: MOO-034.

New competitor, same prompt shape: FLUX 3 Max (fal Research × Black Forest Labs, launched 2026-10-19). fal claims it matches Seedance 2.5's image-to-video Elo (1,139, Artificial Analysis preliminary) at about 22× the speed (12.45 s vs 277.80 s for a 10 s clip). That is a vendor claim. Its official I2V shape is camera move → main action as ordered beats ("then", "as") → secondary environmental motion → light/time change → "Sound:" line. That maps one-to-one onto a Seedance 2.5 first-frame prompt (ratio adaptive), so 17 official FLUX 3 Max examples were ingested today, 14 of them with Seedance 2.5 adapted templates (MOO-031…033, REA-032…034, CAM-090/091, PRF-037/038, PRP-033, WRD-033, AES-034/035/039, GRN-030/031).

Portable stillness and pointer habits from the FLUX 3 Max guide (worth testing in Seedance 2.5 first-frame mode): refer to things already in the frame with "the …" instead of re-describing them; lock unwanted motion with "Nothing else moves" or "The camera holds"; open with "No people." to keep a surreal subject alone (AES-034); write the return ("before they settle back into perfect reflection", MOO-031) to give a quiet shot an arc. Ask for one continuous shot when it matters, because fal saw occasional unrequested cuts.

Film-stock grain wording (official fal examples, adapted for 2.5 in GRN-030/031): "rich 35mm film look with grain and halation, like a 1960s Western", or the longer print-chain description "35mm colour negative … seen as an aged dye-transfer release print … coarse organic film grain, halation around bright edges … faint print dust", paired with exclusions ("No … scanlines, B&W, HDR or digital crispness"). Name the stock and the print, then ban the digital tells.

Cut continuity across hard cuts (official Kling 4.0 example, ported in TRN-030's adapted template): fix the optics ("35mm equivalent, 54° horizontal FOV, locked across all five shots"), camera height and distance, light direction, and say that ambience and music "never reset at the cuts". In Seedance 2.5, put these in the "Keep consistent" line after the timeline.

sections.title: 2026-10-21 additions: prop/staging locks, entity IDs, ports from the BFL FLUX 3 docs

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-21 (about 6 AM PT): the BytePlus Seedance 2.5 prompt guide is still the 2026-10-16 version (the .md copy is byte-identical, md5 40fd6d36…). Runway's 2.5 article (53542207042323, updated 2026-10-13) and 2.0 article (50488490233363, updated 2026-10-15) are unchanged. The only new Runway article in the 40 most recently updated is a general "Why doesn't my generation match my prompt?" FAQ (2026-10-20), with no Seedance specifics. No new official Seedance guidance today; everything below is community practice or ported from other vendors' official docs.

Prop locks and a staging lock (community, Seedance 2.5): give each recurring prop a label and a rule ("PROP-STICK = gnarled dark-brown wooden walking stick, always in Grandma's right hand … PROP-BOWL … never dropped, never changes"), then a STAGING LOCK that fixes who stands where and which path each character enters by ("Leopard later comes up that SAME footpath"). Refer to the labels in the timeline and repeat them in NEGATIVE ("no stick or bowl change"). This fits the official asset-binding step and helps with drifting props in 30 s comedies. Library: PRP-042.

Entity IDs and exact counts (community, Seedance 2.5): with several identical characters, name each one (G1-G5), state the exact count and order ("Exactly five ghosts. Maintain the order G1 → G2 → G3 → G4 → G5"), and give a one-off action to a single ID ("Only G5 waves, exactly once"). The asset block also sets what Image 1 must not contain ("No ghosts in the opening frame") when Image 2 only supplies the look. Library: REA-047.

Ported from BFL's official FLUX 3 audio guide (try in Seedance 2.5; not Seedance documentation): put exact words in quotes and name a visible speaker, or say "voiceover", so the line is spoken rather than printed, and add "no on-screen text or subtitles". Use an "exactly once" line plus a language lock ("every word in French, no English words at all") so the line is neither repeated nor translated back. For a music bed under dialogue, write that the music "keeps playing under and after his words". Name sound sources rather than asking for "quiet room tone", which can collapse into dead air. Library: PRF-046/047/048, REA-042 (adapted templates included).

Ported from BFL's official edit guide (fits Seedance 2.5 edit tasks with ratio adaptive, duration -1, mov): describe only the change, then place what you add (size, look, exact position). Restyle through materials (fibres, seams, compression where the claw grips) instead of a style name. For previz or blockouts, map each grey box to what it becomes and lock "same weave lines, same speeds, same camera overtake". Chain edits: run the second change on the first result rather than stacking both on the source. When replacing dialogue, keep the new line as long as the speech it replaces. Library: PRP-037/038, REA-043/044, MOO-041.

Ported from BFL's continuation recipe (Seedance 2.5 extend task): start by naming what the final frames show ("Continue … from its final frames: the robot reaches the very edge of the workbench"), then say where the shot goes, and carry the established sound unbroken through the seam before adding new sounds. For mechanical subjects, write the imperfection in ("moves like a wound-up machine, not a person: stiff even steps"). Library: TRN-038, PRF-049.

In-prompt cuts (BFL multi-shot recipe, consistent with Seedance 2.5's own multi-shot syntax): consecutive shots must differ strongly, and scale is the strongest difference (macro → wide → aerial). One audio idea spans all shots: a continuous bed plus one sound that scales with the picture ("a tiny crackle … a full roar … a vast distant wash"). Keep 2-3 cuts per generation. For longer films, paste one "world bible" paragraph word for word into every shot prompt and stage one musical motif per shot (enters / warmer / builds / resolves). Library: TRN-034.

Shot-brief header from fal's MiniMax H3 Max example (port in MOO-038's adapted template): Style / Cinematography / Lighting / Color as a 60:30:10 ratio (dominant / secondary / accent) / Camera ("180 degree shutter motion blur", operator shake "motivated by the ground concussions") / Physics ("gravity and inertia respected"), then @subject tags, a LOCATION line, a timecoded ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE block, CONSTRAINTS and an AUDIO (NO MUSIC) list. The 60:30:10 colour ratio is a compact way to state a grade in Seedance 2.5.

sections.title: 2026-10-22 additions: wardrobe locks, motion from frame one, one-take costume changes, ports from LTX-2.5 / Happy Horse / FastH3 / Gemini Omni

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-22 (about 6:15 AM PT): the BytePlus Seedance 2.5 prompt guide is unchanged (the .md copy is still md5 40fd6d36…, the 2026-10-16 version). Runway's 2.5 article (53542207042323, updated 2026-10-13) and 2.0 article (50488490233363, updated 2026-10-15) are unchanged, and none of the 25 most recently updated Runway articles mention Seedance. No new official Seedance guidance today; everything below is community practice or ported from other vendors' official guides.

Wardrobe lock block (community, Seedance 2.5): give the garment its own section, split into parts (bodice / sleeves / skirt / veil, each with fabric, trim and placement), then one hard rule: "The gown must remain identical in every shot. No changes in neckline, embroidery, sleeve design, pearl placement, or veil length." Repeat the same garment parts in the negatives ("changing gown design, missing pearl embellishments, distorted lace patterns, changing veil length"). Add a macro shot of the garment detail to the timeline so the model commits to the trim. This is the official asset-binding and consistency step applied to clothing. Library: WRD-038 (15 s, sub-second timecodes).

Motion from frame one (community, Seedance 2.5): open the timeline with "The shot begins with movement already in progress" and close with a requirements block ("The female protagonist must be moving naturally from the very first frame. Do not leave her standing still and staring for a long time"). This targets a common Seedance failure: a static, staring opening second. The same prompt does a cut by occlusion: "The cockpit doorframe quickly sweeps across the frame and completely obscures the camera, creating a seamless spatial transition through occlusion rather than using a conventional hard cut". That follows the official guide's advice to give every transition a trigger point and a method. Library: REA-054.

One-take costume transformation (community, Seedance 2.5): give the change a trigger (a finger snap) and say where the material starts and how it travels ("aged ivory linen bandages with frayed edges … spiral up from his boots, gradually wrapping his entire body"). Change the set at the same time, keep the camera on a backward track with full-body framing, and add "No sliding feet or walking in place". In the creator's output the protagonist is a woman, although the prompt says "a man", so lock the person with a reference image when it matters. Library: WRD-039. For several looks in one clip, give each look its own timecoded beat and say "Only outfit and background change" (MiniMax H3 example, WRD-041; Seedance port in its adapted template).

Expression sheets (community claim, Seedance 2.5; no prompt published): a 25 s one-take of a 90s cel-anime character in a live-action shrine used two photos, two character sheets and two expression sheets as references. The creator reports that the expression sheets kept the face and drawing style stable before and after a transformation. Worth testing as extra reference_image inputs when a transformation tends to drift the face.

Ported from LTX-2.5 (fal official guide; try in Seedance multi-shot): at every cut, name the edit ("hard cut", "match cut"), re-establish the shot from scratch (scale, lens, light), re-identify returning characters with the exact words used first ("the woman in the bronze silk gown", not a pronoun), and state what the sound does at the cut. For dialogue, let the face arrive first: a beat of stillness before the line gives lip-sync something to lock onto. Keep every sound locatable ("not visible, but locatable"). Library: WRD-037, PRF-055, GRN-038.

Ported from Happy Horse 1.1 (fal official guide): pin each spoken line to its own timecode ("0-4s: … says: \"…\" 4-8s: … answers: \"Friday.\"") and keep lines short. Two clipped lines across a cut stay in sync, while one long line drifts. Treat the audio line as a spotting sheet and write "no music" outright. For a spec ad, write the edit into the prompt (three timecoded cuts) and end on a clean frame with empty lower-third space for a logo added in post. Library: PRF-054, TRN-048, MOO-049.

Ported from Reactor's FastH3 guide and Google's Gemini Omni guide (other models; test in Seedance): each continuation should open on a described hard cut ("Hard cut to a wide shot of …") and re-describe the whole scene, because chained one-takes degrade. In edits, add "Keep everything else the same" after a one-line change. FastH3 also warns that negatives like "No crowds, no text" can summon crowds and text, so name the positive state instead ("an empty platform"). That conflicts with Seedance's official negatives step, so keep Seedance negatives short and concrete. Library: PRF-056, REA-049.

sections.title: 2026-10-23 additions: the official API tutorial and the official sd25-pe skill (section templates, compatibility gates, keyframe sentences, sound symbols)

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-23 (about 6 AM PT): the BytePlus Seedance 2.5 prompt guide is unchanged (.md copy still md5 40fd6d36…, the 2026-10-16 version), and Runway's 2.5 (53542207042323) and 2.0 (50488490233363) articles are unchanged, with no new Runway Seedance methodology. New today: two official BytePlus sources not ingested before, the API "Dreamina Seedance 2.5 tutorial" and the full text of the sd25-pe prompt-optimizer skill (until now the guide only mentioned that it exists). Everything in this section is official unless labelled community.

Task types (official tutorial): text-to-video; first frame / first+last frame (ratio must be adaptive); and omni reference, split by prompt intent into reference, edit (ratio adaptive, duration -1, source video 4-30 s) and extend (ratio adaptive). Set omni_reference_task_type to reference / edit / extend / auto to validate early. If the model reads the prompt as a different task, you get InvalidParameter.TaskTypeMismatch. A parameter clash gives InvalidParameter.TaskTypeConstraint. Trigger words: edits need "edit the video", "add", "delete/remove" or "modify/replace/change"; extensions need "extend forward/backward", "continue" or "continue the story". Edit output can be up to 0.4 s shorter than the source.

Limits (official tutorial): up to 50 references (30 images + 10 videos + 10 audios); pure-audio reference with no image or video is new in 2.5. Durations 4-30 s or -1; 1080p output is 10-bit. output_format mov = H.264, yuv444p, PCM audio (for edit/extend round-trips). 11 languages: Chinese, English, Spanish, Indonesian, Malay, Thai, Arabic, Portuguese, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean. Model ID dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628. Library: TRN-051 (30 s one-take through six rooms, 8 images), PRP-044 (cookie ad, 1 image + 6 videos; asked for 15 s, published output 26.3 s), CAM-108 (extend into a gallery and a painting), PRF-057 (multilingual rap MV).

Official cut technique (multilingual example): "Use HARD CUTS on the beat, with dual contrast on every cut (both shot size and camera type change at the same time)", then numbered shots with [0:00-0:03] ranges. Changing two things at every cut keeps fast cutting readable. Library: PRF-057.

sd25-pe rule 1: keep ratio, duration, resolution and fps out of the prompt body; they belong in API parameters. Do not add quality packs ("8K, masterpiece") or generic negatives the user did not ask for. Only keep exclusions the brief actually needs. The adapted templates from 2026-10-23 follow this: parameters sit on the API line only.

sd25-pe basic template: one line with subject + action + scene, then separate lines for visuals, camera and sound. Camera formula: move + subject + start position + direction + arrival. Write specialist terms as what is visible (rack focus = "focus moves from the cup to her face"; vignette = "edges fall to near black"). Emotion: show it through face, body and pace, not adjectives. Spatial relations are anchored to stable objects ("left of the window"), not screen-left/right.

sd25-pe reference template, in this order: 【Generation Goal】 → 【Reference Asset Roles】 (one asset, one role, one line each; no "Images 2-5" range mappings) → 【Unused Assets】 (list every uploaded asset you don't use, or the model may bring it back) → 【Subjects and Relationships】 (one line per subject) → 【Event Script】 (start state, principal event, end state) → 【Maintain Consistency】. When roles are ambiguous, priority is user statement > prompt > asset content > filename > upload order.

sd25-pe compatibility gate for edits: if the target ratio differs from the source, or the duration differs by more than about 0.3 s, it is not an edit. Write it as a reference task and add "Please note that this is not video editing." right after the goal sentence. For real edits, name @Video1 the "sole editing master", list only the changes, then close the scope: "Except for the objects explicitly modified above, all other visible characters, props, and background elements in @Video1 remain unchanged and are not to be replaced or removed." Replaced motion takes the old motion's slot, and the timeline is inherited. (The skill says ±0.3 s; the tutorial says output may be up to 0.4 s shorter.)

sd25-pe extensions: forward extension continues from the source's last frame; backward extension defines the source's first frame as the end state to reach. Add a single-instance sentence (each person or object appears once) so the seam doesn't duplicate anyone. Keyframes use exact standalone sentences: "Use @Image1 as the first frame." / "Use @Image2 as the last frame."; for several: "Use @Image1 through @ImageN as keyframes in that order." Storyboard grids: at most 15 panels, with the reading order stated.

sd25-pe long videos and timing: split into stages with one state change each. Time ranges are event budgets, not frame-accurate cues, so don't claim 0.5 s precision or invent timestamps from the duration parameter. Products: initial state → operation → observable result.

sd25-pe sound symbols: (music), <sound effect>, {dialogue}, 【subtitle】. For speech, give language + accent + delivery + speaker, then {the line}. The skill's worked example has the non-speaking character "naturally close his mouth and wait". If <> marks sound effects, don't also put <> around names. This makes the community <SFX> habit (TRN-032) official. Community example: REA-055 (@Ziha_ai) binds assets by name ("Image1 is CAR … Image2 is NORA"), tags SFX with <…> and writes "hard cut on every timestamp".

Community, Seedance 2.5 (2026-10-21/23): (a) MiniDV texture from the device, not a filter: "16:9 standard-definition softness, mild video noise, limited dynamic range, imperfect autofocus, exposure shifts … accidental zooms" while ruling out "4K sharpness, heavy grading, VHS overlays" (GRN-039, GRN-041). (b) Voiceover without lip movement: say it twice ("does NOT talk or lip-sync — mouth closed and still; the voice is off-screen narration") (PRF-059). This matches the skill's worked example, where the silent character closes his mouth. (c) Fights: fix screen geography and the 180° rule, give distances in meters and time each strike and reaction (PRF-058). (d) Outputs can ignore "no logo": MOO-052 asked for a plain cap and got a brand logo, so check close-ups.

sections.title: 2026-10-24 additions: Draft mode in practice, the edit example's locked parameters, blockout-to-final and home-video recipes

items.text: Re-checked 2026-10-24 (about 6 AM PT): the BytePlus Seedance 2.5 prompt guide (.md md5 40fd6d36…) and the API tutorial (md5 3ea0e876…) are unchanged since 2026-10-23, and the sd25-pe skill is still v0.1.1 (agent-skills index unchanged; read only, not installed or run). Three tutorial examples skipped last run were reviewed again. None became library entries: the first/last-frame example is minor-coded and its prompt does not match the media; in the Draft example the subject is an age-ambiguous "girl"; the edit example's protagonist is a small figure in a frilly dress and bonnet, seen only from behind. Their parameters are summarised below.

Draft mode (official tutorial): step 1 sets draft=true and only 480p is accepted. It is billed like a normal 480p video. The draft task ID is valid for 7 days from created_at. Step 2 makes the final from the draft task ID and currently supports 1080p only. It reuses the draft's model, prompt, input assets, seed, audio setting, ratio and duration, so freeze the prompt once the draft looks right. Step 2 is billed at the target resolution; any input-video duration is counted from step 1 and the draft video itself is not counted. Draft mode is Seedance 2.5 only (not 2.0 / fast / mini). Workflow: iterate on 480p drafts for blocking, shot order and motion, then make the final once.

Edit example (official tutorial): prompt "Video edit: remove everyone in @Video1 except the protagonist." with a single reference_video. ratio is adaptive and duration -1, and neither can be changed for edits. output_format mov keeps an edit/extend round-trip lossless. The 5:4, 16 s input came back as 5:4, about 16 s. The prompt is one sentence: the task word ("Video edit"), the operation ("remove") and an exception ("except the protagonist"). Everything else is inherited from @Video1, as in the sd25-pe "close the scope" rule from 2026-10-23.

Output specs, official vs news: the API tutorial (as of 2026-10-24) lists Seedance 2.5 output as 480p/720p 8-bit and 1080p 10-bit H.265/HEVC, with 4K (10-bit) listed only under Seedance 2.0. On 2026-10-23 an X news account reported a "Seedance 2.5 4K" release with 10-bit colour and 480p Draft previews. Treat 4K for 2.5 as unconfirmed in the official API docs until the tutorial changes. News only, not used in templates.

Community, blockout to final (CAM-113, @ABAOProductions, 2026-10-22): an untextured, colour-coded Cinema 4D animation goes in as <<<Video1>>> for motion only, with image references for the first frame, the helicopter and the pilot. The prompt then pins camera policy ("EXTERIOR ONLY"), exact crew count, rotor states second by second, and a long "Do not" list built from earlier failures. The creator reports that Seedance read propeller motion much better from a motion-blurred render than from a plain playblast. Their final had shake, grade, film noise and SFX added in Premiere. In sd25-pe terms this is a reference task (not an edit): give @Video1 one role ("motion and camera path only; ignore its colours and untextured surfaces") and list unused assets.

Community, home-video texture written as who filmed it (GRN-042 Seedance 2.5; GRN-043/GRN-044 Wan 3.0, same idea): "shot like a real home video a friend filmed on a cheap consumer DV camcorder from the early 2000s … not cinematic, not a short film", then a list of artefacts (autofocus that searches, washed colours, visible compression, small accidental zooms, no gimbal) and location sound only. "Filmed by another person, never a selfie" stops the model drifting into phone-selfie framing. This adds to the 2026-10-23 MiniDV notes (GRN-039/041). The Wan 3.0 versions add a "Motion quality" block (no teleporting objects, consistent object count) that carries over to Seedance as plain consistency lines.

Community, transformations in one continuous shot (TRN-054): tie each change to a visible trigger (a pumpkin pulse, a candy landing in the mouth) and one sound cue (a crystal bell chime), and say the shot never cuts.
